# Multiple Data Products {#sec-composition}

A platform begins to emerge when one checked product can become the source of another.

## Product dependencies

Products can be nested as sources. Shared dependencies are executed once per execution context in the current core model.

A small dependency graph might look like this:

![The running insurance example as a graph of checked products and derived products.](../diagrams/product-graph.svg){#fig-dependency-graph fig-alt="Policies and brokers feed a portfolio product. The portfolio and payments products feed a monthly performance product."}

The important distinction is that the arrows represent **product dependencies**, not necessarily copied files. A dependency may be an in-memory result, a pinned release, or an adapter-backed source.

## Composition with a lookup

For a single main table plus reference data, a recipe lookup is often simpler than a general multi-source graph.

```{.r}
monthly <- dr_product("monthly_portfolio", policy_delivery) |>
  dataraft.core::dr_add_recipe(
    dataraft.core::dr_recipe() |>
      dataraft.core::dr_step_lookup(brokers, by = "broker_id", name = "brokers") |>
      dataraft.core::dr_step_summarise(
        premium = sum(premium),
        .by = region
      )
  )
```

## Relational models

Core also supports `dm` model products for related tables and declared relationships. A `dm` input creates a model product whose member tables can be checked together. `dr_model()` can construct a relational model from pinned lake releases.

Use this when preserving relationships is part of the product meaning. Do not flatten related tables merely to fit a single-table abstraction.

## Dependency discipline

A dependency graph is useful only when identity is stable. Name products by business meaning, not by temporary file location. Pin releases when reproducibility matters. Keep preparation local to the product that owns the resulting meaning.

This is how a collection of R scripts starts to become a platform: products depend on other products through explicit interfaces rather than undocumented file paths.

## Composition should preserve product boundaries

A dependency graph is useful when each node has meaning on its own. If `policies.validated` is independently useful, a downstream `portfolio.monthly` product can consume it as a product rather than reimplementing its validation. The upstream result then carries its own contract, evidence, and identity into the larger workflow.

DataRaft supports products as sources of other products. Within one execution, shared dependencies are evaluated once. This provides a natural way to express a small directed graph without forcing the user to adopt a separate orchestration service for the first local workflow.

Do not turn every dplyr step into a product. A product deserves an identity when it has at least one durable reason to exist: a consumer boundary, an independently meaningful contract, a release lifecycle, a separate owner, or a reusable result. Internal preparation steps usually belong inside a recipe.

### Relational products

Some interfaces are inherently relational. DataRaft uses `dm` for model products that contain related tables and declared keys. A `dm` input to `dr_product()` creates a model product, and member contracts can be supplied by table. The member tables and relationships are checked together and published as a unit where the backend supports the model publication path.

This is different from flattening everything into one wide table. Keeping a relational model can preserve grain and reduce duplication. It also makes relationship constraints explicit.

The same dependency structure is shown in the figure above. As the project grows, keep this graph understandable before adding more infrastructure.

If this graph is difficult to explain, adding a lake, catalog, or orchestrator will not make it clearer. Start by making product boundaries and dependencies legible in R. Infrastructure should strengthen an understandable model rather than compensate for an unclear one.

## Exercises

1. Build two source products and a third product that depends on both. Draw the resulting graph before executing it.
2. Introduce a dependency cycle intentionally and predict where validation should reject it.
3. Pick a join in an existing analysis and decide whether the joined result deserves its own product identity. Use row grain and downstream reuse as your criteria.
